questions.stem: You are the team leader in birth suite room 1. A 24-year-old woman gave birth vaginally 40 minutes ago and is still bleeding heavily with clots. Help has been called. On palpation the fundus is soft, boggy and above the umbilicus. The placenta was checked and is complete. What is your immediate manual action?
options: Perform a speculum examination to look for a cervical or vaginal tear
Rub up a contraction with fundal massage and expel clots from the uterus
Begin bimanual uterine compression with a fist in the anterior fornix
Explore the uterine cavity manually at the bedside for retained tissue
questions.why: A soft, boggy fundus means atony (Tone). The first manual step is to rub up a contraction with fundal massage and expel clots, done alongside emptying the bladder and giving uterotonics.
notes: You do inspect for trauma, but with a soft fundus the uterus has to be contracted first. Here inspection showed only a graze.
Bimanual compression is the next manual step if bleeding continues despite fundal massage and uterotonics. It is not the first thing you do.
The placenta and membranes were checked complete. Manual exploration needs anaesthesia and is done in theatre, not as a first bedside step.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old, 40 minutes after vaginal birth, has lost 1,500 mL and is still bleeding with HR 140 and BP 90/50. Fundal massage and uterotonics are under way. Bloods show fibrinogen 2.3 g/L, INR 1.1 and platelets 168. How should tranexamic acid be given?
options: 1 g IV, but only if a repeat fibrinogen falls below 2 g/L
2 g orally now, repeated after 6 hours if bleeding persists
1 g IV over 10 minutes now; a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 min
1 g IV over 10 minutes, starting once crossmatched blood arrives
questions.why: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes should be given as soon as possible, and within 3 hours of birth, in every PPH. Give a second 1 g if bleeding continues after 30 minutes. The benefit falls the longer it is delayed.
notes: Tranexamic acid is not held back for a low fibrinogen. It is given early in all PPH, and fibrinogen is replaced separately with cryoprecipitate.
An oral dose is too slowly absorbed for a woman who is actively bleeding and in shock. The IV route is standard.
Tranexamic acid should not wait for blood products. The benefit falls with every delay, so give it now alongside resuscitation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with a major primary PPH has lost about 1,500 mL in 40 minutes and has HR 140 and BP 90/50. Her booking Hb was 124 g/L. The first Hb, taken when the cannula went in, is 96 g/L. Why does this early Hb underestimate how much blood she has lost?
options: Splenic contraction releases stored red cells and raises the Hb for the first few hours
An erythropoietin surge releases reticulocytes quickly, which hides the fall in Hb
Whole blood is lost, so Hb falls only as plasma refill and IV fluids dilute what remains
The lower Hb of pregnancy has a dilutional floor, so the Hb cannot fall any further
questions.why: Acute haemorrhage loses cells and plasma together, so the Hb concentration barely changes at first. It falls only over hours as interstitial fluid moves into the vessels and crystalloid is given. Transfuse on the clinical picture and ongoing loss, not on the early Hb.
notes: Splenic red cell reserve is small in humans and does not explain the gap; the main reason is that whole blood is lost.
Erythropoietin-driven reticulocytosis takes days to appear, not minutes, so it cannot mask an acute fall.
There is no floor stopping the Hb from falling. Pregnancy haemodilution lowers the baseline, but Hb can still fall steeply as the blood is diluted.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old has a major PPH from uterine atony that is not responding to uterotonics and a balloon tamponade. The consultant asks interventional radiology to embolise the uterine arteries, reaching them through the femoral artery. Which vessel do the uterine arteries arise from?
options: The posterior division of the internal iliac artery
The ovarian artery, a branch of the abdominal aorta
The anterior division of the internal iliac artery
questions.why: The uterine artery branches from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. It runs in the base of the broad ligament and crosses above the ureter beside the cervix. This is the target for embolisation and for surgical ligation in PPH that does not respond to treatment.
notes: The external iliac artery supplies the lower limb and gives the inferior epigastric artery, not the uterine artery.
The posterior division gives parietal branches (iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal), not visceral pelvic branches.
The ovarian artery joins the uterine artery near the cornua, but the main supply to the uterus is the uterine artery from the internal iliac.
